title: Trump’s Golf Course: A Hearing Diary for Oct. 19
gist: A Lawfare liveblog of the Oct. 19, 2026 evidentiary hearing before Judge Ana Reyes on Trump's plan to replace East Potomac's public golf course, in which Interior and NPS witnesses were pressed on why 400+ healthy trees were cut Oct. 10 and DOJ was challenged over reversing its prior NEPA and final-agency-action positions.

themes.theme: Trump plan versus government's litigation position

insights.claim: Two days before the hearing government attorneys called plans for the course 'conceptual', 'nascent' and 'preliminary', yet Trump said he was closing the existing course Nov. 15 or earlier and a later post said work would begin 'IMMEDIATELY'.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: The gap between presidential statements and court filings undermines the government's credibility.

insights.claim: DOJ told the court the agency's position is there is no final plan, that no contract with Fazio exists, and that Trump's posts should be read like an executive order to be carried out consistent with law.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: The government's no-final-plan stance is the main defense against injunction.
insights.locator: agency's position is, there's no final plan

insights.claim: Judge Reyes stressed that DOJ and sworn NPS declarations had for months said any redesign would be major federal action requiring NEPA review and an environmental impact statement, and called switching arguments now unacceptable.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Prior sworn statements constrain DOJ's new argument that no agency action exists.
insights.quote: not acceptable to make one argument for months and months and months and then when that ends up being inconvenient to switch arguments

insights.claim: DOJ's final-agency-action position is that a manager's directive on routine maintenance is not agency action, analogized to a Smithsonian director rearranging exhibits; when pressed, DOJ could not name a case with so narrow a view or give the facts of its two cited cases.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Weak precedent support increases the odds of an injunction and appellate scrutiny.

themes.theme: Tree cutting and the contradictory record

insights.claim: On Oct. 10 NPS cut more than 400 healthy, non-invasive trees at East Potomac, some dating to the 1920s, which the government said was done under a 2019 Cultural Landscape Report and tree management plan unrelated to Trump's redesign.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Core factual dispute; a finding of pretext would support a preliminary injunction.

insights.claim: Judge Reyes said she did not think trees were cut because of the 2019 report and planned to find they were cut to effectuate the Washington National Plan, adding witnesses may not have been lying and may have been told otherwise.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Signals likely adverse preliminary ruling on the tree removal.
insights.quote: i plan at this moment to make finding that trees were cut down to effectuate WNP

insights.claim: Interior deputy chief of staff Gregory Wischer testified he learned of the 2019 report only in mid-to-late September, never read it fully, read only the East Potomac portion, and acknowledged tree clearing was the only element of the report implemented Oct. 10 beyond fencing and clean-up.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Selective use of the report supports the pretext inference.

insights.claim: NPS acting director Jessica Bowron testified she learned of the report Sept. 29, approved the tree plan after only a 'fatal flaw' review, and signed a declaration at 5:15pm Oct. 6, 24 minutes before approving the plan, that made no mention of removing 400+ trees.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Undercuts reliability of government declarations to the court.

insights.claim: Bowron said the tree plan became possible because of an incoming team and the fiscal-year turnover, and Griess said the roving crew freed from reflecting pool work was reassigned; the government cites resource availability, not the golf plan, for timing.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Timing explanation the court found unpersuasive.

insights.claim: Superintendent Kevin Griess conceded the vast majority of trees were healthy and that none of the structural problems from his May declaration or the report's drainage and bunker recommendations had been addressed.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog

insights.claim: Wischer testified he toured the course with Trump, Tom Fazio and NPS deputy director Frank Lands, carried Fazio's conceptual proposals, received design sketches by text on his personal phone from Gavin Fazio, and first saw the sketch Trump later posted on the Thursday before the hearing.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Direct design input from Trump's chosen architect undercuts 'no plan' claims.

insights.claim: Judge Reyes ordered Wischer not to delete anything and to turn off auto-delete on his personal phone, and said she wants briefing on whether third parties like Fazio waive executive privilege.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Discovery of Fazio communications could further expose planning.

insights.claim: DOJ's Stan Woodward asserted attorney-client and deliberative process privilege over the Oct. 5 meeting, and Reyes laid out a test (pre-decisional, deliberative, not purely factual), saying lawyer presence does not make a conversation privileged.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Privilege rulings will determine how much planning evidence emerges.

insights.claim: Reyes called it impossible that the tree cutting and the golf plan coincidentally happened together, rejecting Woodward's 'both can be true' with 'not dealing with quantum physics here'.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Judge openly skeptical of the government's coincidence story.
insights.quote: There is no universe where all of this just coincidentally happened at the same time.

insights.claim: DOJ argued plaintiffs lack standing for an aesthetic or design claim and that the Supreme Court's Seven County decision requiring deference bars the NEPA segmentation claim; Reyes noted Judge Amy Berman Jackson read that decision as limited to EIS cases.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: The scope of Seven County deference is a key appellate question.

insights.claim: Plaintiffs, including DC Preservation League and regular golfers, argue recreational injury from destruction of the three Travis-designed courses, and asked for a longer notice window before irreversible changes and before course closure plus a bar on further tree removal.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Narrow relief of notice and tree-removal halt is the likely injunction.

insights.claim: Judge Reyes said she was very unlikely to order everything stopped and asked what the equities are against a notice requirement given the government says there is no urgency and no plan to close.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog

insights.claim: An amicus brief for Haines Point Runners argued the three-mile perimeter roadway is historic and would be eliminated, and that 40 U.S.C. 8106 bars building on national park land without congressional approval.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Congressional-approval statute could be an additional legal obstacle.

insights.claim: Judge Reyes said she is receiving death threats over the case and called that not what the founders envisioned.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Reflects mounting pressure on judges in administration litigation.
